title: VRCX-K Host Ready
description:
The host → shell startup handshake: the host announces that its kkrpc/ws surface is listening, how to authenticate to it, and the environment it is running in. This is the FIRST frame the host sends, so it is versioned like every other cross-boundary DTO — a shell that does not recognise `schemaVersion` must refuse the handshake rather than connect to a surface it cannot speak to.

WHY THE ENVIRONMENT IS HERE AT ALL: the Rust shell and the frontend are separate processes; neither can call `process.platform` for the host. A host-local PLUGIN can, so these fields are explicitly NOT for plugins — they are for the remote consumers (the shell, the face, and the LAN/mobile clients that `docs/mobile-feasibility.md` §2 reserves). Metadata a plugin can read for itself does not belong on the wire.

STALENESS: `capacity` fields are a snapshot taken at handshake time. `ready` is sent exactly once per host process, so a field whose value changes minute-to-minute would be read as a constant. Dynamic values (free memory, live RSS, uptime) are deliberately absent and belong to the `host-lifecycle` snapshot feed or a dedicated query.

schemaVersion.description: Version of THIS handshake. Bumped only for a breaking shape change; the shell rejects a value it does not implement, which is what turns 'version-skewed sidecar' from a silent half-start into a named failure.

port.description: TCP port the host's kkrpc/ws server bound on 127.0.0.1. It binds port 0 and reports the port the OS assigned, so this is always a concrete connectable port — never 0.

token.description: Per-launch bearer token (32 random bytes, lowercase hex) that the ws client must present as `?token=`. The pattern is part of the contract, not a stylistic preference: a truncated or uppercased token would be rejected by the host's own comparison, so catching it here names the real fault.

hostVersion.description: The host build's own version (the same value the ws API `getVersion()` returns, and the one the host already prints in its `ready` log line). Carried here because the shell supervises the host but otherwise has NO way to learn which build it is supervising: `getVersion()` is reachable only over the ws connection the face opens later.

runtime.description: The JavaScript runtime the host is executing on. A plugin author reads these to know which APIs are available; the shell records them in crash reports.

bunVersion.description: Bun version string (e.g. `1.4.2`). Bun is the host's engine, so this is the version that decides most API availability.

nodeVersion.description: The Node compatibility version Bun reports (e.g. `v26.3.0`). Distinct from `bunVersion`: code checking Node-compat behaviour needs this one.

host.description: The host's platform identity. `platform`/`arch` deliberately reuse the vocabulary already fixed by `contracts/plugin-manifest/v1` rather than the raw `process.*` spellings, so the two contracts cannot drift into two names for the same machine.

platform.description: Operating system only, and deliberately coarse — the ARCHITECTURE is a separate axis (`arch`), exactly as plugin-manifest defines them. NOTE this is NOT `process.platform`: the raw values are `win32`/`darwin`, and emitting those would create a second vocabulary for the same fact.

arch.description: CPU architecture, using plugin-manifest's names rather than `process.arch` (`x64`/`arm64` coincide today, but pinning OUR names means a Node rename cannot silently change the wire).

mode.description: How the host was launched. `compiled` = the single-file `bun build --compile` sidecar shipped with the app (`Bun.isStandaloneExecutable`); `source` = run from a checkout (`bun run dev:host`). This is NOT cosmetic: in `compiled` mode the process cwd is the resource directory (`docs/adr-plugin-layout.md`), so `paths.cwd` means something different than it does in a dev session — a consumer reading `paths` must consult this field to interpret it.

paths.description: Where the host is running from. Absolute paths, and therefore personally identifying (they contain the OS user name). They ride this handshake because it currently terminates on this machine, but any client reachable over a network must treat this object as sensitive — see `docs/mobile-feasibility.md` §2, where the face becomes remote.

cwd.description: The process working directory. Interpret it together with `host.mode`: packaged runs set it to the resource directory, dev runs to the checkout root.

execPath.description: Absolute path of the running executable. In `compiled` mode this is the sidecar itself; in `source` mode it is the `bun` binary, which is how a sideloaded/duplicate host is spotted.

capacity.description: A SNAPSHOT of the machine's capacity, taken when this handshake was built (`capturedAtMs`). Only values that do not meaningfully change while the process lives are included: a consumer sizing a cache or a worker pool wants these, and they stay true for the process lifetime. Deliberately EXCLUDED because they change minute-to-minute and would be misread as constants in a once-per-process frame: free memory, live RSS, process uptime, and load average — the last one is additionally useless here, because `os.loadavg()` returns `[0,0,0]` on Windows (measured).

capturedAtMs.description: Unix epoch milliseconds when this snapshot was taken. REQUIRED as a sibling of the values it dates: without it, `capacity` in a long-lived log reads as 'current' rather than 'as of handshake'.

cpuCount.description: Logical processor count (`os.cpus().length`), not physical cores. The number a worker-pool sizing decision should use.

totalMemBytes.description: Total physical memory in bytes. Exceeds 32 bits on ordinary machines (measured: 33,676,386,304 here), so it is a plain JSON integer bounded by the repo-wide safe-integer ceiling rather than a u32.

propertyNames.description: camelCase, because these keys are field-shaped additions rather than a free-form bag.

additionalProperties.description: Scalars only. Nested objects/arrays are excluded on purpose: an open EXTENSION POINT is not the same as an unbounded sub-schema, and a scalar forces a promotable shape — anything that grows structure should be promoted to a named field with its own boundary instead of deepening this one.

extra.description:
Forward-compatibility slot, and the reason the top level can stay strict. The named groups above are the fields we know we need TODAY; this is how a future addition (another runtime fact, a build identifier, a capability flag) travels without a schema-version bump and without weakening `additionalProperties:false` on the groups.

BOUNDED ON PURPOSE: `maxProperties` plus a camelCase key rule keeps this from becoming a dumping ground, and scalars-only keeps the unvalidated surface narrow. The repo's precedent for this style is `plugin-manifest`'s `Dependencies` open map — a `maxProperties`-capped, key-constrained `additionalProperties` — rather than an unchecked free-for-all.

Reading rule for consumers: treat `extra` as advisory. A key's presence is not a compatibility promise, and its absence never means the feature is unavailable. Anything a consumer must branch on belongs in a named group.
